item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts decided to drop Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the lineup for Game 3 of the National League Division Series amid the designated hitter’s ongoing struggles.
Ohtani was 2-for-8 in the series entering play Tuesday against the Atlanta Braves. Having a tough left-handed assignment on the mound in Chris Sale influenced Roberts’ decision, and Ohtani completely bought in.
“Runs are going to be hard to come by. We all understand that,” Roberts began. “Sale’s going to be tough. But the guys I feel at the top have a good chance to get on base, and I do think that there’s going to be opportunities where the game, the situation, bleeds into Shohei’s at-bat.
“So I had a good conversation with him last night, told him my thoughts. And he completely understood and in all honesty, he said, ‘I was going to come to you in September and say, why don’t you hit me seventh?’ My point being, he wants to do whatever will help the team.
“So I feel good about this today. And it’s nothing as a sign of what’s more to come. It’s just for today specifically.”
The flow of the game played perfectly into the Dodgers’ strategy, as Ohtani was given prime RBI opportunities twice within the first three innings. But the results were not what Roberts had hoped for.
The Dodgers’ star struck out in the first inning to strand a runner in scoring position, but he did reach on catcher’s interference later in the third.
Because of the relationships Roberts has built with his players, he was not surprised Ohtani took the news well. While it was a difficult decision, Roberts felt it gave his team the best chance to counter Sale and the pitchers coming in after him.
“Not surprised at all. And I think that from day one, I’ve always said that my job is to do whatever is best for the team. And so I know I’ve built the equity and the trust in the players,” he said. “And so today I just feel this gives us the best chance to beat the Braves today and combat Sale, to combat what they’re going to throw after Sale. I feel good about it.”
The Dodgers’ skipper also hoped the change would help Ohtani stay within himself better than he has.
“I use that a lot, where it might give him a different look, let the game come to him a little bit later. I don’t think it’s a pressure thing. I do think it’s something where he wants to do more. But in that same breath, I do think that there’s going to be a couple big spots today where he’s going to be at-bat,” Roberts said.
Although Sale presents a wholly unique challenge for any left-handed hitter, Ohtani chased plenty out of the zone in the first inning. The Braves starter attacked the outside part of the plate and effectively tunneled his fastball and slider to get Ohtani to chase.
Ohtani worked a 3-0 count in his third at-bat against Sale but lost a challenge on what he thought was ball four and proceeded to get beaten by a fastball inside for a flyout.
Rather than signaling a lack of confidence, Roberts believes Ohtani nearly initiating the lineup change himself is an example of self-scouting.
“He’s a very good self-evaluator, a very high competitor and expects a lot from himself. I still think he’s very confident. But Sale’s a different monster. He’s tough, certainly, against lefties. But I still think he’s confident,” Roberts said.
“So now with that, just getting him back in the zone, and that’s easier said than done, I understand that. But there’s going to be high velocity trying to crowd him in to then spin him off. Is Shohei willing to take the knock to left field as he did against Dodd? So those are the things you’re looking for tonight.”
Shohei Ohtani’s lineup spot in Game 4
The Braves have right-hander Tyler Mahle on the mound to start against Tyler Glasnow in Game 4. However, Roberts said that does not necessarily guarantee that Ohtani will be back in the leadoff spot.
“Mahle is certainly a neutral, you could argue a reverse. So I don’t know that answer. Yes, he does throw with his right hand, but I haven’t made that decision quite yet,” he said.
Roberts did not specify if Ohtani’s at-bats on Thursday would tip the scale one way or the other, but the Dodgers’ skipper did confirm that the left-hander would not be batting in the fifth spot again.
If you love our reporting, choose DodgerBlue.com as a preferred source on Google.

item.content:encoded:
7 de octubre de 2026 - 9:45 PM
Atlanta - Yoshinobu Yamamoto ponchó a 10 bateadores en siete entradas, Enrique “Kike” Hernández conectó un jonrón de dos carreras y los Dodgers de Los Ángeles vencieron 3-1 a los Braves de Atlanta el martes por la noche, tomando una ventaja de 2-1 en su Serie Divisional de la Liga Nacional.
Hernández, quien suele brillar en octubre, sacudió su decimoséptimo cuadrangular en postemporada, quebrando un empate con el miembro del Salón de la Fama de Béisbol Carlos Beltrán.
El boricua ahora está empate con Jim Thome, Aaron Judge y David Ortiz en la lista de jonrones en la postemporada.
Yamamoto dominó el muy esperado duelo contra el as de Atlanta, Chris Sale, quien permitió tres carreras y siete imparables en cinco entradas. Yamamoto, Jugador Más Valioso (MVP) de la Serie Mundial de 2025, concedió solo cuatro hits y una base por bolas, mejorando su récord de postemporada a 8-1.
Los Dodgers pueden ganar la serie —pactada al mejor de cinco juegos— y dar un paso más en su intento de convertirse en el primer equipo de la Liga Nacional en ganar tres títulos consecutivos de Serie Mundial si vencen nuevamente a los Braves el miércoles por la noche en el cuarto partido.
Los Braves esperaban que dar descanso adicional a Sale fuera una fórmula ganadora para este crucial tercer encuentro. Sin embargo, tras dejar a seis corredores en base en las primeras tres entradas, permitió el jonrón de dos carreras de Hernández y un cuadrangular solitario de Freddie Freeman en el cuarto episodio.
Ozzie Albies abrió la novena entrada de Atlanta con un doblete contra el muro entre el jardín derecho y el central ante los lanzamientos de Edwin Díaz, avanzando a tercera base tras un rodado de out de Michael Harris II. Díaz dejó al corredor varado cuando Mauricio Dubón fue puesto out en un elevado de foul al jardín derecho y Mike Yastrzemski fue retirado con un rodado al campocorto Mookie Betts.
Tras una temporada agobiado por lesiones, Díaz se apuntó su primer salvado desde el pasado 14 de agosto, cuando lanzó la novena entrada en blanco contra Milwaukee.
FUe además su primer rescate de postemporada desde el 14 de octubre de 2024, cuanto se apuntó un salvamento por los Mets de Nueva York contra los propios Dodgers en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Nacional.
Dubón realizó una atrapada saltando sobre la barda del jardín izquierdo para robarle un jonrón a Freeman en la tercera entrada; sin embargo, Freeman logró conectar su cuadrangular una entrada más tarde. El jonrón de Hernández hacia el jardín izquierdo impulsó a Andy Pages, quien había conectado un sencillo. Un out después, Freeman conectó el jonrón número 18 de su carrera en postemporada hacia el jardín derecho, ampliando la ventaja a 3-0.
El mánager de los Dodgers, Dave Roberts, bajó al bateador designado Shohei Ohtani al quinto puesto del orden al bate, debido a que Ohtani registraba un promedio de 3 de 15 en su carrera contra Sale. Ohtani se había ido de 4-0 con dos ponches ante Sale cuando los Dodgers perdieron 1-0 el 26 de agosto en Atlanta. Roberts predijo acertadamente que Ohtani tendría oportunidades con corredores en base al batear en una posición más baja del orden de bateo.
En la primera entrada, con corredores en primera y segunda, Sale ponchó a Ohtani para cerrar el episodio. En la tercera, con dos corredores en base, Ohtani llegó a primera gracias a una interferencia del receptor Drake Baldwin —lo que llenó las bases—, antes de que Miguel Rojas terminara la entrada con un elevado al jardín derecho. Ohtani recibió una base por bolas al abrir la octava entrada frente a Brent Suter, el cuarto lanzador de Atlanta.
Un rodado de Baldwin a primera base, con las bases llenas, impulsó a Dubón —quien había conectado un sencillo— en la quinta entrada, anotando así la única carrera de Atlanta ante Yamamoto.
Rojas abandonó el partido durante un turno al bate en la octava entrada. El segunda base pareció lastimarse la espalda al realizar un swing y fue sustituido por Tommy Edman. Los Dodgers informaron que la lesión consistía en dolor en la zona lumbar.
Tanner Scott sumó dos ponches en una octava entrada sin anotaciones para Los Ángeles.
Las noticias explicadas de forma sencilla y directa para entender lo más importante del día.

item.content:encoded:
ドジャースの山本由伸が6日（日本時間7日）、敵地で行われたブレーブスとのナ・リーグ地区シリーズ第3戦に先発。7回を4安打1失点、1四球、10奪三振に抑え、3―1の勝利に貢献した。ドジャースは対戦成績を2勝1敗とし、リーグ優勝決定シリーズ進出へ王手をかけた。
大谷翔平、地区シリーズ初戦は4打数1安打 初回に快音
1勝1敗で迎えた第3戦は、ブレーブスの左腕クリス・セールとの投げ合いとなった。山本はポストシーズンで自身最多となる10三振を奪い、相手打線を封じた。
打線は四回、エンリケ・ヘルナンデスの2ランとフレディ・フリーマンのソロで3点を先取。山本は五回に1点を失ったものの、七回まで追加点を許さず、リードを救援陣につないだ。
八回はタナー・スコット、九回はエドウィン・ディアスが無失点に抑えた。投打がかみ合ったドジャースは、先に3勝したチームが勝ち上がる地区シリーズで、突破まであと1勝に迫った。
まるスポ編集部

item.title: [WSLS] Yamamoto is dominant again as Dodgers ride homers from Hernández and Freeman to 3-1 win over Braves
item.dc:creator: Charles Odum; Associated Press
item.description: ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning. “I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator. Recommended Videos The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason. Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlan
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA – Yoshinobu Yamamoto felt trust from Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts when he remained in a crucial NL Division Series game after a stressful fifth inning.
“I’d like to continue living up to the highest expectation,” Yamamoto said through a translator.
Recommended Videos
The right-hander from Japan continues to do more than just meet expectations in the postseason.
Yamamoto struck out 10 in seven brilliant innings, Kiké Hernández hit a two-run homer and the Dodgers beat the Atlanta Braves 3-1 on Tuesday night to take a 2-1 lead in their NL Division Series.
Yamamoto dominated his much-anticipated matchup with Atlanta ace Chris Sale, who allowed three runs and seven hits in five innings. Last year's World Series MVP permitted only four hits and one walk while improving to 8-1 with a 2.14 ERA in 11 career postseason outings, including 10 starts.
His 10 strikeouts were a postseason high for him.
“I was confident and able to control all my pitches today,” Yamamoto said.
The Dodgers can clinch the best-of-five series and take another step toward becoming the first National League team to win three consecutive World Series by beating the Braves again Wednesday night in Game 4.
Atlanta hoped giving Sale extra rest would be a winning formula in the pivotal third game. Instead, after stranding six runners in the first three innings, he gave up the two-run homer to Hernández and a solo shot to former Braves star Freddie Freeman in the fourth.
“He was still touching 100 (mph),” manager Walt Weiss said of Sale. “The stuff was fine. Like I said, maybe the command not perfect. It wasn’t bad. But they did a nice job against him.”
That was all the offensive support Yamamoto and relievers Tanner Scott and Edwin Díaz would need.
Ozzie Albies opened the Atlanta ninth with a double off the right-center wall against Díaz and moved to third on Michael Harris II's groundout. Díaz stranded the runner and earned a save when Mauricio Dubón fouled out to right field and Mike Yastrzemski grounded out to shortstop Mookie Betts.
A homer for the boo birds
Freeman said he didn't mind being booed by Atlanta fans in the sellout crowd of 42,420.
“I’ve got a gray uniform on,” Freeman said. “I expect boos. It’s OK. ... It’s all love. I still love everybody here and I’m looking forward to tomorrow.”
Dubón made a leaping catch over the left-field wall to rob Freeman of a home run in the third. Freeman wouldn't be denied an inning later. Hernández's homer to left drove in Andy Pages, who singled. One out later, Freeman pulled his 18th career postseason homer to right field for a 3-0 lead.
Lineup change
Roberts moved designated hitter Shohei Ohtani down to No. 5 in the lineup because Ohtani was 3 for 15 in his career against Sale. Ohtani went 0 for 4 with two strikeouts against Sale when the Dodgers lost 1-0 on Aug. 26 in Atlanta.
Roberts correctly predicted Ohtani would have opportunities with runners on base hitting lower in the order.
With runners on first and second in the first, Sale struck out Ohtani to end the inning. With two runners on base in the third, Ohtani reached on catcher's interference by Drake Baldwin to load the bases before Miguel Rojas ended the inning with a flyball to right field. Ohtani walked to lead off the eighth against Brent Suter, Atlanta's fourth pitcher.
Baldwin's bases-loaded grounder to first base drove in Dubón, who singled, in the fifth for Atlanta's only run.
Injury report
Rojas left during an at-bat in the eighth. The second baseman appeared to injure his back on a swing and was replaced by Tommy Edman. The Dodgers announced the injury as lower back pain.
Roberts said Rojas probably won't start on Wednesday and his availability off the bench will be determined before the game.
“I give him credit for conceding that at-bat,” Roberts said.
Weiss made a late change, moving Ronald Acuña Jr. from right field to designated hitter. Weiss said Acuña jammed his knee on a slide in Game 2. Acuña remained in the game but the knee was sore on Tuesday, leading to the lineup change.
Milestone win for Roberts
Roberts now has 71 career postseason wins, tying Tony La Russa for second-most in major league history. Joe Torre is first with 84.
Up next
Braves right-hander Tyler Mahle is expected to face Dodgers right-hander Tyler Glasnow in Game 4 on Wednesday night. Mahle said Tuesday an abdominal pull is now a “non-issue.” He felt the pull before allowing one run in seven innings of a 4-3 loss to Philadelphia in 10 innings during the NL Wild Card Series last week.
___

item.title: [MLB.com] Dubón le niega un jonrón a Freeman... pero Freddie cobra revancha después
item.dc:creator: Paul Casella
item.description: Después de que Sale consiguiera cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en el Juego 3 de la SDLN contra los Dodgers, Dubón registró el primer out defensivo y lo hizo de manera espectacular. Con un corredor en primera y nadie fuera en la parte alta del tercer inning, la exsuperestrella de los Bravos Freddie Freeman conectó un batazo profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo que salió de su bate a 101.3 mph. item.content:encoded:
Después de que Sale consiguiera cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en el Juego 3 de la SDLN contra los Dodgers, Dubón registró el primer out defensivo y lo hizo de manera espectacular.
Con un corredor en primera y nadie fuera en la parte alta del tercer inning, la exsuperestrella de los Bravos Freddie Freeman conectó un batazo profundo hacia el jardín izquierdo que salió de su bate a 101.3 mph. Dubón siguió la trayectoria de la pelota hasta la pared y calculó perfectamente su salto para realizar la atrapada justo frente a un grupo de relevistas de los Dodgers, quienes se preparaban para que la bola cayera en el bullpen de los visitantes.
La atrapada de Dubón probablemente le robó un posible jonrón de dos carreras a Freeman, pero como mínimo evitó un extrabase y, casi con toda seguridad, una carrera o dos en el episodio.
Los Dodgers llenaron las bases gracias a un sencillo de Will Smith con dos outs y a que Shohei Ohtani llegó a salvo por interferencia del receptor, pero Sale salió ileso al hacer que Miguel Rojas conectara una línea al jardín derecho para terminar la entrada.
Antes de siquiera necesitar la ayuda de su defensa, Sale se unió a Mike Hampton (Juego 2 de la SDLN del 2003) como los únicos lanzadores de los Bravos en conseguir cada uno de sus primeros seis outs por la vía del ponche en un juego de postemporada.
Freeman se desquitó en su siguiente turno al bate, cuando disparó con autoridad un cuadrangular hacia el jardín derecho-central, el 18vo vuelacercas de su carrera en postemporada, para darle a los Dodgers una ventaja de 3-0.

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Dodgers beat Braves on Kiké Hernández and Freddie Freeman homers, take 2-1 NLDS lead

item.content:encoded:
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — The Dodgers went into Game 3 of the National League Division Series knowing they couldn’t be so reliant on the home run, especially with Braves ace Chris Sale on the mound. And yet, in a 3-1 win, it was the home run ball, paired with a masterful performance on the mound from right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto, that secured the victory.
The Dodgers pulled ahead to a 2-1 lead in the best-of-five series.
The Dodgers tried to score in other ways, putting on six baserunners in the first three innings of the game. But it didn’t work.
They failed to take advantage of some luck and poor defense from the Braves in the first inning, as Mookie Betts beat out a soft ground ball up the first base line and Teoscar Hernández reached on a fielding error by Braves shortstop Ha-Seong Kim.
Yoshinobu gives up four hits and strikes out 10 and Kiké Hernández hits a two-run home run to power the Dodgers to victory in Game 3 of the NLDS.
The lineup shuffling manager Dave Roberts did against Sale had superstar Shohei Ohtani, batting fifth, walking up to the plate with two outs and runners on first and second. His over-anxious approach at the plate so far this postseason followed him into the at-bat. And he struck out whiffing on a slider in the opposite batter’s box.
The next inning, Kyle Tucker hit a two-out single into left, baited Sale into picking over to first base twice, and then stole second. But he was stranded there, as Kiké Hernández went down swinging. All six of the Dodgers’ outs in the first two innings came via the strikeout.
In the third, the Dodgers loaded the bases. Mookie Betts started the effort with a double through the left side of the infield. And it looked for a moment as if Freddie Freeman had capitalized on the opportunity with a runner in scoring position.
He stayed back on a fastball and crushed it to deep left field, on a trajectory to just clear the short fence. But Braves left fielder Mauricio Dubón made a leaping catch, holding into the ball as he slammed into the wall.
Undeterred, the Dodgers kept putting runners on base. With two outs, Will Smith stayed through a slider to single. Ohtani clipped Braves catcher Drake Baldwin’s mitt and was awarded first base for catcher’s interference. Then Miguel Rojas, who’d exit the game in the eighth inning mid-at-bat with what the Dodgers called low back pain, hit a line drive that found leather to end the inning.
So, back to the long ball.
Perennial postseason hero Kiké Hernández delivered the first blow. With Andy Pages on first, after his first hit of the series, Hernández launched a changeup into the left-field stands. Then, two batters later, Freeman turned on an inside sinker and sent it over the right-field fence — where Dubón had no chance to track it down.
Game 3 was billed as a matchup between aces: Sale, whom the Braves tabbed for Tuesday because of his workload in their wild-card series, and Yamamoto, whom the Dodgers partially held back for the first two games with the NLCS in mind.
Yamamoto held up his end of the bargain, limiting the Braves to four hits and one run in seven innings.
He retired 10 of the first 11 batters he faced. The only baserunner in that time, Michael Harris II, bunted for a single. Yamamoto crashed hard, slipping on the slick grass as he tried to pivot but still managing to make a throw to first from the ground.
Shohei Ohtani is batting fifth in the lineup against Braves ace Chris Sale in Game 3 of the NLDS. He hasn’t hit fifth or lower in a starting lineup since 2020 with the Angels.
He only wavered in the fifth, loading the bases with a pair of singles and a four-pitch walk. The Braves’ batting order turned over, and Yamamoto got Baldwin to ground out to first, but that allowed a run. Then he induced Ronald Acuña Jr. to ground out to second to escape the jam. Rojas ranged to his left to field the ball and made an on-target throw even as he slipped on the grass in shallow right field.
Yamamoto didn’t allow another baserunner.
Left-handed reliever Tanner Scott served as the Dodgers’ setup man, throwing a hitless eighth. And right-hander Edwin Díaz came in for his first save opportunity since Aug. 14 against the Brewers.
He gave up a double off the wall to Ozzie Albies to open the inning but retired the next three batters.

item.content:encoded:
Freddie Freeman and Kiké Hernández continue to add to their postseason résumés.
An inning after Freeman was denied an opposite-field home run over the left field wall at Truist Park by Mauricio Dubón, he thought he might try hitting one right.
But Hernandez needed to show off his bat first.
The two got the Dodgers on the board, to give them a 3-0 lead in the fourth inning of the NLDS, by hitting home runs over the walls in left and right field.
Hernández saw an 89 MPH changeup come his way by Braves starting pitcher Chris Sale and sent it 406 feet out of the park for a two-run homer. One batter later, Freeman obliterated a 96 MPH sinker and sent it screaming off the bat at 103 MPH for 399 feet.
Sale managed to get out of the inning in the following at-bat, but at first glance, it looked he was going to gve up another homer.
Teoscar Hernández just came short of Sale’s slider out of the park, after hard-hitting Sale at 108 MPH.
Both Freeman and Hernandez, continue to show why they are dominant in October, as both of them have had playoff heroics.
Freeman has a career batting average of .268 with 82 hits, 17 home runs, and 40 RBI through 81 postseason games.
Kiké Hernández has a career average of .272 with 80 hits and 16 home runs, with 42 RBIs in the postseason.
The combination of Hernández and Freeman came on the same day; manager Dave Roberts made a surprising decision to bump four-time MVP Shohei Ohtani down to the fifth hole in the Dodgers lineup and have Freeman hitting second, behind Mookie Betts, while Hernández was hitting ninth.
So far, his decision is paying off as Los Angeles holds a 3-1 lead against the Braves.

item.content:encoded:
When will Dodgers' Tarik Skubal pitch next in NLDS? Here's the latest update appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The Los Angeles Dodgers are currently gearing up for Game 3 of their NLDS series against the Atlanta Braves on Tuesday afternoon on the road. The Dodgers are currently tied 1-1 with Atlanta after dropping a frustrating contest in Game 2 at home over the weekend.
The Dodgers won Game 1 of this series thanks in large part to a dominant pitching performance from ace Tarik Skubal, and now, the latest reporting has revealed when Skubal could be on the mound again for Los Angeles.
"Tarik Skubal throwing bullpen session in preparation for his next start…possibly Game 5," reported David Vassegh of AM 570 LA Sports on X, formerly Twitter.
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
Of course, if the Dodgers have their way, they'll win the next two games in Atlanta and avoid a Game 5 altogether, in which case Skubal would likely be the starter for Game 1 of the ensuing NLCS.
However, Los Angeles certainly has their work cut out for them in order to make that scenario a reality. Los Angeles' main hitters, headlined by Mookie Betts and Shohei Ohtani, have largely been dormant so far in this series, with the team mustering just two runs in Sunday's loss to Atlanta despite the Braves running out an all-bullpen lineup.
On Tuesday, Los Angeles will face off against the formidable Chris Sale, who is coming off a long rest after Walt Weiss opted not to rush him back in Game 2 in a gutsy move that ended up paying off.
The Dodgers will certainly want to see their bats come to life in Game 3 to retake control of the series.
Game 3 between the Dodgers and Braves is slated to get underway at 6:00 pm ET from Atlanta.
Related: Why Joe Davis isn't on broadcast for Fox's Dodgers-Braves NLDS Game 3

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are tied with the Atlanta Braves at one game apiece in their best-of-five series in the NLDS.
On Tuesday night, the two teams will meet for Game 3 at Truist Park in Atlanta, with the Braves sending out left-handed ace Chris Sale while L.A. will start right-hander Yoshinobu Yamamoto in what should be one of the best pitching matchups we’ve seen so far this postseason.
Ahead of the game, Dodgers manager Dave Roberts made some major lineup changes, including one involving veteran slugger Freddie Freeman.
Dodgers Announce Freeman Move
With Shohei Ohtani struggling at the plate recently, Roberts decided to move him down to the No. 5 spot in the lineup Tuesday night.
As a result, Freeman will move up from the cleanup spot to the No. 2 spot, while Mookie Betts remains in the leadoff spot.
Teoscar Hernandez and Will Smith will fill the No. 3 and No. 4 spots, while the back end of the order will remain fairly close to what the Dodgers have used recently, despite bringing Andy Pages back into the lineup.
Here’s the full Dodgers lineup:

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Shohei Ohtani dropped to fifth in Dodgers' batting order for Game 3 of NLDS vs. Braves
item.dc:creator: Chris Cwik
item.description: The Los Angeles Dodgers are pushing two-way star Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the batting order following a tepid start to the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves. After hitting second in the first two games of the series, Ohtani was dropped to fifth ahead of Game 3 on Tuesday. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernández and Will Smith will hit ahead of Ohtani in Game 3. In the two previous games in the series, Betts led off and Ohtani hit second. Per The Athletic's Fabi
item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers are pushing two-way star Shohei Ohtani to fifth in the batting order following a tepid start to the National League Division Series against the Atlanta Braves.
After hitting second in the first two games of the series, Ohtani was dropped to fifth ahead of Game 3 on Tuesday. Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman, Teoscar Hernández and Will Smith will hit ahead of Ohtani in Game 3.
In the two previous games in the series, Betts led off and Ohtani hit second.
Per The Athletic's Fabian Ardaya, Dodgers managers Dave Roberts told reporters that the move to fifth would be just for Tuesday's game against Braves ace Chris Sale. A lefty, Sale has been notoriously tough against left-handed batters over his career.
Roberts added that when he approached Ohtani about moving down in the order on Monday, Ohtani responded that he'd considered suggesting doing so in September as he struggled through injuries.
Hitting fifth is unusual for Ohtani, who hasn't hit that low since 2020, when he was a member of the Los Angeles Angels.
Ohtani hasn't been terrible in the first two games of the series, going 2-for-8 with two strikeouts. But other members of the team have outperformed the slugger in the NLDS. Freeman and Hernández, in particular, have ignited the Dodgers' offense. Smith, however, is hitless in eight at-bats thus far.
At the plate, Ohtani has been worse against lefties over his career, though he still has an excellent .853 OPS against them. That's actually higher than Smith's career OPS against left-handers.
Ohtani, however, came into the playoffs battling multiple injuries. On Friday, he acknowledged that left knee and right biceps issues will impact him throughout the postseason. Those same issues seemed to affect Ohtani in the second half, as he hit .241/.322/.472 in August before collapsing with a .200/.300/.233 line in eight games in September. At that point, the team put Ohtani on the injured list to give him time to recover for the playoffs.
Now that the playoffs are here, the Dodgers will try to ease Ohtani into a bigger role. While he hit second in the order early in the NLDS, a combination of his performance and Sale's presence on the mound will drop Ohtani much lower than he has hit in recent seasons.

item.title: [ABC7 Los Angeles] Dodgers land two-time Cy Young winner Tarik Skubal in blockbuster deadline deal, sources say
item.dc:creator: Alden Gonzalez
item.description: LOS ANGELES -- For as much as they might have downplayed the possibility behind closed doors, the Los Angeles Dodgers were long seen by rival executives as overwhelming favorites to land generational ace Tarik Skubal. Their farm system was too good, their goals were too lofty, their rotation had become too uncertain. On Saturday night, a day and a half before the trade deadline, they pulled it off. item.content:encoded:
LOS ANGELES -- For as much as they might have downplayed the possibility behind closed doors, the Los Angeles Dodgers were long seen by rival executives as overwhelming favorites to land generational ace Tarik Skubal. Their farm system was too good, their goals were too lofty, their rotation had become too uncertain.
On Saturday night, a day and a half before the trade deadline, they pulled it off.
The Dodgers acquired Skubal, the reigning back-to-back American League Cy Young Award winner, from the Detroit Tigers for a package of three prospects: outfielder Zhyir Hope, and right-handers River Ryan and Brady Smith, sources told ESPN's Jeff Passan.
Skubal, a 29-year-old pending free agent, will now headline what was arguably already the best rotation in the sport. Alongside him will be Yoshinobu Yamamoto, making a strong case for a Cy Young of his own, followed by Blake Snell, Shohei Ohtani and Tyler Glasnow, all of whom are in varying stages of returning from injury.
The Dodgers had long touted their depth as a reason they didn't necessarily need Skubal. Snell, who has made one start all year, is expected to rejoin the rotation after his next rehab outing. Glasnow, out since May 6 with back spasms, will begin a minor league rehab assignment next week. And though Ohtani is still troubled by a sore left knee that only seems to bother him on the mound, Dodgers president of baseball operations Andrew Friedman said earlier this week he fully expects him to pitch in October.
The Game 1 starter, though, will be Skubal, who might be the best pitcher in the world.
Skubal boasts a 2.79 ERA in 16 starts this year, striking out 116 batters and issuing 14 walks in 96 innings. The only thing that could stop him were bone chips that began to cause irritation in his left elbow in late April. Skubal underwent a less-invasive, revolutionary NanoScope procedure and returned in about six weeks. His ERA in July is 2.03. And as he addressed the media in the visiting clubhouse at Sutter Health Park in Sacramento late Saturday night, moments after being informed of the trade, Skubal at one point got choked up.
"Going into the season, this isn't what I planned on doing," Skubal said before getting on the verge of tears while reflecting on his time in Detroit. "But circumstances change, situations change. I'm very appreciative of everything that the Tigers have done for me."
A late bloomer who lasted until the ninth round of the 2018 draft, Skubal began to emerge as one of the game's most talented pitchers in 2022 and 2023 and took it to another level thereafter. From 2024 to 2025, Skubal went 31-10 with a 2.30 ERA and a whopping 469 strikeouts in 387 innings. His 12.6 FanGraphs wins above replacement led all major league pitchers.
When Skubal and members of the Tigers' front office exchanged arbitration figures in the ensuing offseason, the two sides were $13 million apart. An independent arbitrator ruled in favor of Skubal and his agent, Scott Boras, rewarding him a $32 million salary as he headed into his free-agent year.
Rumors had swirled throughout the offseason that the Tigers would trade him then. Instead, they doubled down, signing fellow starter Framber Valdez to a three-year, $115 million contract with the hope of winning the AL Central. Instead, the Tigers flopped. By the end of May, they were tied with the Colorado Rockies for the worst record in the majors, prompting executives throughout the industry to assume Skubal would be traded.
The Tigers proceeded to win 28 of their next 46 games, and suddenly it seemed as if Skubal might stay. But their momentum ran out. The Tigers lost back-to-back games to the last-place Kansas City Royals over the weekend and dropped two of three to the Baltimore Orioles thereafter. The last of those losses, on Wednesday night, saw Skubal take the mound and record his 1,000th career strikeout, then sit in the dugout while his team blew a 7-0 lead.
After it was over, the Tigers were seven games below .500, six games out of first place and three games out of a wild-card spot.
To many observing Skubal's availability, it was a death knell to his time in Detroit.
The Atlanta Braves, Chicago Cubs, Milwaukee Brewers, New York Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays were all in on Skubal to some extent, with the Brewers, deep in prospects, the favorites among that group. But the Dodgers were the clear frontrunners all along. And now they'll add Skubal to a laundry list of talent they've acquired from the outside over the years, following Ohtani, Snell, Yamamoto, Glasnow, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and, this offseason, Edwin Diaz and Kyle Tucker.
The vast majority of those players came via free agency. The Dodgers loathe the high asking prices at midseason. But in getting Skubal, they parted from an outfield group that is stocked with talent -- one that is still headlined by Josue DePaula, a consensus top-25 prospect, along with Eduardo Quintero, ranked 45th on Kiley McDaniel's latest ESPN rankings. They also maintain all of their young major league starting pitching, namely Justin Wrobleski, Emmet Sheehan and Roki Sasaki.
In Hope and Ryan, though, the Tigers came away with two top-50 prospects.
Hope, 21, was slashing .293/.369/.530 with 23 home runs and 18 stolen bases for the Dodgers' Double-A affiliate and brings explosive power from the left side, top-tier speed and an ability to handle center field.
Ryan, 27, made a brief stint in the major leagues in 2024, putting up a 1.33 ERA in four starts. He then underwent a prolonged rehab from Tommy John surgery and has made eight starts in Triple-A, putting up a 4.46 ERA. He has been out since the middle of June with a hamstring injury, but McDaniel ranked him 49th in his midseason top 50 in May.
Smith, 21, was a third-round pick out of high school in 2023 who has put up a 3.88 ERA in 19 starts at the Class A level this season.
In three months, Skubal will head into the open market with the chance of signing the most lucrative deal ever rewarded to a starting pitcher. Before then, he will join a Dodgers club that boasts the highest run-differential and second-best record in the major leagues -- and help them try to become the first team in NL history to win three consecutive championships.
Asked his thoughts about joining the Dodgers, Skubal took about 15 seconds to compose himself before saying: "Yeah, it's exciting. I'm excited. They've got a good group."

item.content:encoded:
As Shohei Ohtani works his way back to being in top form on the baseball diamond, the star continues to make off-field moves. Through the first two games of the NLDS against the Atlanta Braves, Ohtani is hitting .250 with two hits and two strikeouts.
During the Dodgers’ run in the MLB playoffs, New Balance announced that Ohtani’s signature clothing line is now available in select markets.
“Shop the latest styles from the Shohei Ohtani Signature Collection,” New Balance noted in an October 3, Instagram post featuring Ohtani.
“Available now in select markets.”
Additionally, Chandler Bats announced that select fans can purchase a game-model bat designed for Ohtani. These will be a hot commodity as only 1,000 are being released.
“The bat behind the player who changed the game,” Chandler Bats noted in an October 1, Instagram post tagging Ohtani.
“Introducing the SO17.4 Limited Edition — built to @shoheiohtani game-model specifications and crafted by Chandler, available to the world for the first time,” Chandler Bats added.
“Only 1,000 will be made. Sign up to be the first to know at the link in bio.”
Shohei Ohtani’s Contract With Dodgers Includes $68 Million Deferred Annually Starting in 2034
Ohtani signed a massive 10-year, $700 million contract with the Dodgers that is slated to go through the 2033 season. One of the interesting aspects of Ohtani’s deal is that a large portion of the money is deferred.
According to Spotrac, Ohtani will receive $68 million annually from 2034 through 2043. It will be interesting to see what impact this will have on the Dodgers’ potential roster moves during this future time period.
With the way Ohtani’s deal is structured, it allowed the Dodgers to be more aggressive at the MLB trade deadline landing star pitcher Tarik Skubal as one example.
Dodgers Star Shohei Ohtani Is Projected to be MLB’s Top Earner in 2026 at $127 Million
SAN FRANCISCO, CALIFORNIA – SEPTEMBER 25: Shohei Ohtani #17 of the Los Angeles Dodgers walks back to the dugout after striking out against the San Francisco Giants in the top of the eighth inning at Oracle Park on September 25, 2026 in San Francisco, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images)
Ohtani is projected to earn $127 million in 2026, the highest of any baseball player, per Forbes. The star is projected to earn $125 million through endorsements and business ventures compared to $2 million with the Dodgers.
“It’s no wonder that brands are still clamoring for his services, and he recently added a partnership hawking Japanese firm Kirin’s immune health supplements to his long list of sponsors,” Forbes detailed.
“With support like that, Ohtani’s $127 million estimated earnings will exceed the combined totals of the Nos. 2 and 3 players on this year’s Forbes list, with Cody Bellinger and Kyle Tucker set to bank $112.5 million between them.
Injuries have complicated the star’s 2026 campaign, but Ohtani is a rare phenom with the ability to be both an elite hitter and pitcher. This is only going to continue to allow Ohtani’s net worth to grow.

item.title: [Dodgers Way] Kiké Hernández’s unusually serious answer to Dodgers’ place in lockout proves players won’t budge
item.dc:creator: Matthew Swigonski
item.description: Despite an injury-plagued season for Shohei Ohtani, 2026 has been a really good year for the Los Angeles Dodgers. After signing Kyle Tucker in the offseason and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline, they loaded up their roster yet again en route to the second best record in all of baseball. But with the Dodgers painted as the “bad guy” over the last few seasons, the team may ultimately have a major say in the potential 2027 lockout. With a total luxury tax payroll of over $420 million,
item.content:encoded:
Despite an injury-plagued season for Shohei Ohtani, 2026 has been a really good year for the Los Angeles Dodgers. After signing Kyle Tucker in the offseason and trading for Tarik Skubal at the trade deadline, they loaded up their roster yet again en route to the second best record in all of baseball. But with the Dodgers painted as the “bad guy” over the last few seasons, the team may ultimately have a major say in the potential 2027 lockout.
With a total luxury tax payroll of over $420 million, the Dodgers spent more money than the four lowest-spending in the league combined. Not only has that drawn the ire from opposing fan bases, but it puts the Dodgers into the spotlight regarding the Major League Baseball Collective Bargaining Agreement negotiations. The owners are eyeing a salary cap to curb spending. But that’s a concept that players like Kiké Hernández refuse to entertain.
As reported by Andy McCullough of The Athletic, the Dodgers clubhouse has not been immune to feeling the burn of that ire and the pressure of a potential lockout next season. But that doesn’t mean that the players are getting desperate. Hernández even acknowledged that the guys in the Dodgers clubhouse know exactly how the game is played on and off the field.
“Whenever things like a CBA come around, there always has to be a bad guy in order for the opposition to want to change things,” Hernández told The Athletic. “And we just happen to be the ones to blame, at this point. Obviously, probably well-deserved, because of the way the last couple of years have gone. Especially with the spending.”
Obviously that spending has paid off for the Dodgers, but does it put them at an unfair competitive advantage?
Kiké Hernández feels like the Dodgers are doing things the right way
Outside of the COVID-shortened season in 2020, the Dodgers have not had a payroll under $200 million since 2018. But as we’ve seen with teams like the New York Mets, spending money doesn’t always equate to a World Series title, or even fielding winning teams that can make it to the postseason.
But with the opportunity to win their third consecutive World Series and their fourth in seven seasons, the Dodgers have spent their money the right way. They’ve made the majority of their acquisitions count and they haven’t taken on too many bad contracts in recent years. The team even boasts a strong minor league system with affordable players like Josue De Paula.
Granted, the deferred money with Ohtani’s contract is the mother of all workarounds, but they still played by the rules when finalizing that deal. That is something that Hernández feels like every team should be doing.
“If you own a team, it would make sense that you’re trying to make that team the best possible, in order to win,” added Hernández. “Because if not, you’re just treating the team as a stock. And why would you want to compete against other people if you’re just trying to make money? Sell the team to somebody who actually wants to compete and win.”
Obviously professional sports are a business. A multi-billion dollar business at that. But at the heart of that business is a game. As Hernández describes it, the Dodgers are just out to win that game and collect another ring. Other teams may lack the budget to stretch their payroll like the Dodgers, but who is most to blame for that?
As of this season, there are just two MLB owners who don’t have a net worth of at least a billion dollars. Bob Castellini of the Cincinnati Reds has $400 million to his name and Dick Monfort Colorado Rockies has a net worth of $700 million. So there is plenty of money to go around baseball. It just comes down to who is willing to spend it in order to win. And winning is something that the players don’t want to negotiate on.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Shohei Ohtani, Hank Aaron Award finalist, still searching at the plate
item.dc:creator: Eric Stephen
item.description: Dodgers designated hitter has won the Hank Aaron Award, the honor given annually to the top offensive player in his league, in each of the previous three seasons, in 2023 with the Angels then in 2024-25 in his first two years with the Dodgers. Ohtani won't win it this season, but he's a finalist again, and deservedly so. item.content:encoded:
Dodgers designated hitter has won the Hank Aaron Award, the honor given annually to the top offensive player in his league, in each of the previous three seasons, in 2023 with the Angels then in 2024-25 in his first two years with the Dodgers. Ohtani won't win it this season, but he's a finalist again, and deservedly so.
Now the Dodgers need Ohtani to find something, anything at the plate as they try to break a 1-1 tie in the National League Division Series against the Braves.
Ohtani has two singles in eight at-bats during the NLDS, and since returning from the injured list on September 23 has seven hits, including a double, in 29 at-bats, with one walk and a strikeout. There was the September 24 game against the Padres in which he consistently hit the ball hard, but other than that Ohtani hasn't gotten any real results at the plate for seven weeks.
He last homered on August 18 at Coors Field, and in 94 plate appearances since is hitting a paltry .160/.277/.198.
Ohtani was clearly diminished at the plate just before landing on the injured list four weeks ago, after dealing with left knee inflammation and a right biceps injury. All sides seem to agree Ohtani is not 100 percent, but when asked if his injuries would require offseason attention, Ohtani didn't offer much in response.
"I haven't been able to get a good grasp of the root cause of all this. I think that process is going to happen during the off-season when I'm going to have a little bit more time to be able to address it," Ohtani said, through interpreter Will Ireton, last Friday on the eve of the NLDS. "But as of now, it's something I'm just going to have to manage."
We probably won't know the full extent of Ohtani's maladies this season until some Instagram post with a considered-font graphic detailing whatever procedure he might have had once the season is done. But for now, if we take Ohtani and the Dodgers at their word and he is healthy enough to play, he hasn't helped himself by chasing. Ohtani swung at seven pitches outside the strike zone in Game 2 alone on Sunday.
"I think that the amount of at-bats leading up to it, it was, I think, five games, I think you still — I felt good about having some at-bats to finish the season, the at-bats that he took in the bye week," manager Dave Roberts told reporters on Monday in Atlanta on the workout day at Truist Park. "But at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone. I don't think that that has anything to do with — he had the five games. He had the at-bats in between. I think that's something that — it's hard to have success when you're out of the zone."
Roberts in that same media session on Monday said he would even consider moving Ohtani even further down in the lineup. Ohtani batted second in two of his five regular season games after getting activated from the injured list and batted second in both NLDS games to date.
In three years with the Dodgers, Ohtani has only batted first or second, with his last time in another lineup spot coming in 2023, with 59 starts batting third for the Angels.
"I think moving him from 1 to 2 — but going further than that? I'm open to it," Roberts said Monday. "And it's something that if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why."
While most of the last month and a half focused on what Ohtani hasn't done, his overall numbers in 2026 were solid, and among the best in the sport. They just happen to pale in comparison to his 54-homer, 59-steal campaign followed by 55 home runs in his first two years with the Dodgers.
Ohtani hit .275/.377/.512 with 30 home runs, a 139 wRC+, 89 runs scored, 81 RBI, and 81 walks in 135 games. He's one of 10 finalists for the National League Aaron Award, which will almost certainly go to Pete Crow-Armstrong.
2026 NL Hank Aaron Award finalists
- CJ Abrams – Washington Nationals
- Jake Bauers – Milwaukee Brewers
- Pete Crow-Armstrong – Chicago Cubs
- Elly De La Cruz – Cincinnati Reds
- Shohei Ohtani – Los Angeles Dodgers
- Matt Olson – Atlanta Braves
- Kyle Schwarber – Philadelphia Phillies
- Sal Stewart – Cincinnati Reds
- Fernando Tatis Jr. – San Diego Padres
- Jordan Walker – St. Louis Cardinals
The Aaron Award, which has existed since 1999, is decided by a panel of "MLB legends and past recipients of the prestigious award" plus fan voting that accumulates into one vote on the panel. The Hank Aaron Award winners in each league will be announced during the MLB awards show on November 11.

item.title: [DodgersBeat] Dave Roberts Ponders Dodger Lineup Tweaks Ahead of Game 3
item.dc:creator: Steve Webb

The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2. With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly. Díaz Could Close “I think that we’ve buil
item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA, GA — Dave Roberts spent Monday weighing changes on both sides of the ball before Game 3 in Atlanta.
The Dodgers manager said he is considering lineup tweaks against Chris Sale, including the possibility of moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the order. He also made it clear that Edwin Díaz has worked his way back into serious ninth-inning consideration after his sharp outing in Game 2.
With the NLDS tied 1-1, Roberts sounded open to adjusting quickly.
Díaz Could Close
“I think that we’ve built him up, regained the confidence in him and himself,” Roberts said of Díaz. “I think that it’s certainly a viable option for tomorrow night. I feel very confident with him finishing a game.”
Roberts said Díaz’s most recent outing was about as good as he has seen from him.
“That last outing was as good as we’ve seen him throw, and it’s hard to imagine throwing any better,” Roberts said. “He’s put himself in a position to be the closer.
“In October, I don’t pay too much attention to the long sample of a season in a lot of cases, because in October things happen quickly and you’ve got to be willing to read and react.”
Roberts also praised the way Díaz handled a difficult season.
“Character,” he said. “That’s the main thing. When things aren’t going the best and how players respond, that’s telling.
“The way he stayed the course, dealt with the injuries, went to OKC on a longer rehab to work things out and then took on whatever role we had for him says a lot about him.”
Lineup Changes Are on the Table
Roberts also acknowledged that the Dodgers could look different against Sale.
“I am considering it,” he said. “I think that’s a very fair question. I have to be mindful of it being two games, and then within those two games, what have I seen? Are we seeing good at-bats?”
He pointed to Will Smith as someone whose results have not matched the quality of his plate appearances.
“I think Will Smith is taking good at-bats, just missing some pitches, taking good swings, not chasing much,” Roberts said. “Versus other people maybe expanding, trying to do too much.
“Those are things that you’re trying to make bets on. Then you’re looking at tomorrow with Sale, the history, recency, how guys are prepared and will prepare for Sale. So yeah, I’m thinking through that, and there are possible changes.”
Roberts listed Kiké Hernández, Miguel Rojas and Max Muncy among the options he could work into the lineup.
“At the end of the day, our guys are our guys,” he said. “I can tweak a lineup. I can insert, take out a player or two, but we still have to go out there and play, execute and take good at-bats.”
Moving Ohtani Is Possible
Roberts said he would consider moving Ohtani further down in the order if he believes it helps the team.
“I would,” he said. “I think moving him from one to two, but going further than that, I’m open to it.
“If I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on. I know that undoubtedly.”
Roberts thinks some of Ohtani’s recent issues have come from trying to do too much.
“I think there’s a little bit of trying to do too much,” he said. “Everything orbits around Shohei in the sense of his talent, and the Braves are going to enter with caution. They’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them.
“Until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to use that playbook.”
He also said Ohtani may be pressing for power.
“Hitting homers, slugging is so much a part of his hallmark in the batter’s box,” Roberts said. “He’s very in tune with what’s being said, what he hasn’t done.
“But that base hit the other way yesterday, that’s production. Against a guy like Chris Sale, that gives you a chance. Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan given the starter.”
Roberts Still Believes in Pages
Andy Pages has also struggled, but Roberts said he plans to keep giving him chances.
“I’m going to continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re going to need him to be an active part of our team.
“This is, for me, given how he has come into the postseason, too small of a sample. He has taken two walks. Tomorrow is not going to be the end-all, be-all because Sale is a tough matchup, but I still want to see good at-bats.”
Roberts believes the main issue is pressing.
“I think there’s trying to do too much,” he said. “When he came back, he was swinging the bat really well, had success, and now I think there’s a little bit of trying too much.”
Freeman Looks Healthier
One hitter Roberts feels especially good about is Freddie Freeman.
“I think he’s gotten into his legs a lot more,” Roberts said. “He’s moving balls in the hitting zone forward. He’s as healthy as he’s been in quite some time. I think the mechanics are sound.”
Roberts credited the five-day break with helping Freeman get his knee into better shape.
“The week off was really crucial for him,” he said. “Being able to manage that with the five days off got him back to health to be able to work through some things without having to perform in a game setting.”
Sale vs. Yamamoto
Roberts expects Sale to attack the Dodgers much the same way he did when Atlanta faced them in August.
“The fastball just sort of bullied us at the top of the zone,” Roberts said. “There was some chase down below, and with the lefties, throwing more two-seamers to keep us honest in and then expand away.”
Still, Roberts believes the Dodgers are in a better offensive place than they were then.
“I do think we are in a different spot,” he said. “The stakes are certainly higher. There is familiarity on both sides. I think we’ll see better at-bats.
“Chris is going to be tough regardless. We know that. We know we’re going to be in for a dogfight, but I just don’t see him bullying us like he did his last start.”
And Roberts feels good about the pitcher the Dodgers will send out against him.
“There should be a lot of talk about Chris Sale, but our guy’s pretty dang good,” Roberts said. “He’s been a very good pitcher in the postseason, so we feel very good about that.
“I think both pitchers are going to pitch well. It’s kind of who grinds out at-bats best.”

A lifelong baseball fan, Webb has been going to Dodger games since he moved to Los Angeles in 1987. His favorite memory was attending the insane Game 3 of the World Series in 2025 and hugging random Dodgers fans after Freddie’s walkoff homer. He has been writing for Dodgersbeat since 2020.

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers, who are attempting to win their third straight World Series title, were beaten by the Atlanta Braves in the second game of the National League Division Series.
With both games of this series having taken place in Los Angeles, both teams will now travel to Atlanta, where things will resume in Game 3 on Tuesday.
And for the Dodgers, their highest-profile player could soon be moved in the lineup, according to manager Dave Roberts.
The Los Angeles Dodgers Could Move Shohei Ohtani Down In The Lineup
Star Shohei Ohtani is 2-for-8 so far in the postseason, but he chased on over 50 percent of the pitches on which he swung, getting away from the kind of discipline he’s built his career on.
According to Dodgers skipper Dave Roberts, he’s open to moving Ohtani down in the lineup, and would have a conversation with him beforehand to explain the potential move.
“Going further than moving him from one to two, I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “If it’s something I do, I’d obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. Every conversation I’ve had with him that’s whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on it.
“If you look at the AB’s there’s a lot of chase. It’s hard to square up, put good swings on balls out of zone. Sale is going to be tough, trying to get him back in the hitting zone.”
Additionally, Roberts said that Ohtani, who missed time this season, isn’t currently experiencing any health issues.
“I haven’t heard anything other than he feels fine. This time of year everyone doesn’t feel perfect. He’s doing the best he can.
“He’ll be in there Game 3. We just have to take good at-bats and expect the best.”
The Dodgers Were Beaten In Game 2
Following their Game 2 loss, Roberts said that he and his club have their work cut out for them.
“It’s a good team offensively,” he said. “They’re going to fight. (Michael) Harris is swinging a good bat. We knew it was going to be a battle. We knew those guys weren’t going to go down.
“We’re expecting Sale in Game 3, and we’ve got our work cut out. Now it’s a three-game series.”

item.content:encoded:
The Los Angeles Dodgers have faced two bullpen games to kick off their National League Division Series battle with the Atlanta Braves.
On Tuesday, things will get much more difficult.
The Dodgers are going up against 10-time All-Star and former Cy Young award winner Chris Sale. The left-hander is coming off a regular season in which he had a 2.16 ERA and 200 strikeouts over 162.2 innings. He then allowed three runs over 6.1 innings in his wild-card Game 1 start, and pitched 1.1 scoreless innings to close out Game 3.
The Dodgers know what they're up against with Sale, one of baseball's best pitchers.
"Chris is going to be tough," Roberts said. "We know we're going to be in for a dogfight."
The difficult lefty matchup also has manager Dave Roberts considering some lineup changes.
“I think so," Roberts said. "I am considering it. I think that’s a very fair question. I think that I have to be mindful of — it’s two games, and then with the two games, what have I seen?”
Roberts mentioned Enrique Hernandez and Miguel Rojas as potential options to be in the lineup. The only Dodgers with any semblance of success against Sale in their careers are Mookie Betts (7-for-18) and Freddie Freeman (5-for-16).
The Dodgers have been especially reliant on the home run this series, with all seven of their runs coming via the long ball.
In Sunday's Game 2, they went 0-for-8 with runners in scoring position.
Sale faced the Dodgers on Aug. 27, firing a complete-game shutout with 11 strikeouts and just five hits allowed.
Dave Roberts Considering Moving Shohei Ohtani Down in the Lineup
The Dodgers have plenty of players struggling in the lineup, including Will Smith (0-for-8), Andy Pages (0-for-7) and Tommy Edman (0-for-5).
At the top of the lineup, however, is Shohei Ohtani, who is 2-for-8 with two singles and two strikeouts. He's looked far from his usual self.
"I think there's, like we've talked about, he's not 100%," Roberts said on Monday. "But at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone. ... I think that's something that — it's hard to have success when you're out of the zone. ... And Shohei understands, any hitter understands that. So I think that's the thing is — then the question is how do we get him into it? I think there's a little bit of trying to do too much. I think that's a piece."
Roberts said he's open to moving Ohtani down in the lineup, especially with the tough left-hander on the mound.
However, he wouldn't commit to anything on Monday.
"Going further than [No. 2]? I'm open to it," Roberts said. "It's something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day, every conversation I've had with him is, whatever is best for the team, he's all in on.”
For what it's worth, Ohtani is 3-for-15 against Sale in his career with five strikeouts.
"At the end of the day, our guys are our guys," Roberts said. "And, yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats."

item.title: [Los Angeles Times] Move Shohei Ohtani down in the Dodgers' lineup? Dave Roberts is 'open' to it

item.content:encoded:
Move Shohei Ohtani down in the Dodgers’ lineup? Dave Roberts is ‘open’ to it
- Click here to listen to this article
ATLANTA — As the Dodgers mull potential lineup changes for Game 3 of the National League Division Series, manager Dave Roberts said he is “open” to moving Shohei Ohtani lower in the batting order.
In his three seasons with the Dodgers, Ohtani has batted first or second in every game he has started. However, as he has admitted he is trying to “manage” in the aftermath of knee and arm injuries, and as Roberts has acknowledged Ohtani is “not 100%,” the lack of success could compel the manager to replace him at the top of the lineup with a more productive hitter at some point.
“I would,” Roberts said Monday. “I would. I think it’s something that, you know, I think moving him from 1 to 2 — but going further than that? I’m open to it.
“And it’s something that if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. And at the end of the day every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team, he’s all-in on. So I know that undoubtedly.”
It would be strange for the Dodgers to bench Shohei Ohtani, but it’s clear that pretending he’s healthy enough to provide meaningful at-bats isn’t helping.
The Dodgers are batting .215 through the first two games of the NLDS, with the Atlanta Braves scheduled to pitch left-handed ace Chris Sale in Game 3 on Tuesday. If the Dodgers lose, they would need to win back-to-back elimination games to advance beyond this series.
Roberts said the lineup changes he would consider include starting Kiké Hernández and Miguel Rojas, both of whom hit well against left-handers. That could mean infielders Max Muncy (0 for 7 against Sale, with five strikeouts) and Tommy Edman (0 for 11 against Sale) might not start.
Center fielder Andy Pages, who batted so poorly last October he was benched for the final three games of the World Series, is hitless in seven at-bats in this series, with four strikeouts.
“I’m gonna continue to give Andy leash,” Roberts said. “I believe in him. I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.
Roberts said he did not envision benching catcher Will Smith, who is 0 for 8 in the series. The Dodgers’ backup catcher, Hunter Feduccia, is a career .205 hitter with no postseason experience.
But, even with the Dodgers’ star-studded lineup, the spotlight shines brightest on Ohtani.
Ohtani has not homered since Aug. 18. He hit .157 between then and the end of the regular season, striking out in 41% of his at-bats. In this series, he has two hits and two strikeouts in eight at-bats, and his inability to refrain from swinging at pitches outside the strike zone has become a glaring weakness.
“He’s not 100%,” Roberts said. “But, at the end of the day, he can still do a better job of staying in the strike zone.”
Ohtani hasn’t given the Braves a reason to challenge him within the strike zone.
“Everything orbits around Shohei, in the sense of his talent,” Roberts said. “And the Braves are going to enter with caution. And, so, knowing that, they’re going to continue to expand as long as we keep giving that to them. So until we show some discipline, they’re going to continue to kind of use that playbook.”

item.content:encoded:
ATLANTA –– The Dodgers don’t want to overreact to a two-game sample size.
But, with elimination all of a sudden just two games away, they don’t want to wait too long to make changes either.
That’s what dynamic manager Dave Roberts was grappling with on Monday, as the Dodgers gathered at Truist Park in Atlanta ahead of Game 3 of their National League Division Series against the Braves.
A daunting challenge awaits on Tuesday night, when the club will face Braves ace Chris Sale for the first time since he threw a complete-game shutout against them in August.
Thus, even though the team’s quest for a World Series three-peat just began, potential lineup changes were already under consideration.
And even superstar Shohei Ohtani might not be immune.
“I am considering [changes],” Roberts said. “I think that’s a very fair question.”
That didn’t mean Roberts was ready to commit to any significant alterations ahead of a pivotal Game 3, with the best-of-five series tied one game apiece.
He noted the danger of reading too far into small playoff sample sizes this early in the postseason.
Still, he said there were things he was “thinking through” and “possibly kind of some changes” that could be enacted on Tuesday.
One possibility: Inserting Miguel Rojas and/or Kiké Hernández into lineup, perhaps in place of Max Muncy and/or Tommy Edman, to give the Dodgers extra right-handed bats against a dominant left-hander in Sale.
Another, more notable potential option: Moving Ohtani even further down the order from his current No. 2 spot, after he went just 2-for-8 in the first two games of the NLDS while continuing to battle right arm and left knee injuries.
“[We already moved] him from 1 to 2 –– but going further than that? I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “It’s something that, if I do, I would obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why.”
The explanation, of course, wouldn’t be too complicated.
In Ohtani’s currently diminished physical state, he has simply not been the same presence at the top of the order that the Dodgers have grown accustomed to from the four-time MVP.
“Like we’ve talked about, he’s not 100%,” Roberts said.
But also, “I think there’s a little bit of [him also] trying to do too much,” Roberts added. “I think that’s a piece.”
Indeed, Ohtani has suffered from a futile combination so far in the playoffs, failing to either punish pitches over the plate or keep from chasing out of the strike zone.
“It’s hard to have success when you’re out of the zone,” Roberts said. “So I think that’s the thing, then the question is: How do we get him [attacking pitches back] into it?”
A change of mindset could help, especially against a premium pitcher like Sale (who has held Ohtani to a 3-for-15 mark with five strikeouts and only one double in their career head-to-head matchups).
“Trying to chase slug tomorrow night might not be the right plan, given the starter,” Roberts said.
Instead, Roberts pointed to the opposite-field single Ohtani slapped past a shift for his lone hit in Sunday’s Game 2 loss.
“That at-bat yesterday, the block base hit the other way, that’s something that is production,” Roberts said. “I think that’s something where, against a guy like Chris Sale, it gives you a chance.”
The Dodgers, of course, would love to get more pop from Ohtani, who led the team with eight home runs during last year’s World Series trek. Roberts also knows the slugger “feels the responsibility” to provide such power, which might be contributing to his lack of plate discipline.
Thus, for now, taking the pressure off Ohtani’s shoulders by potentially hitting him lower in the lineup might also prove to be prudent.
“At the end of the day, every conversation I’ve had with him is whatever’s best for the team,” Roberts said. “And he’s all in on [that]. I know that undoubtedly.”
While Roberts will contemplate other changes beyond Ohtani’s spot in the order, there were a few ideas he outright struck down Monday night.
The big one: Removing Andy Pages from the batting order despite his 0-for-7 start in the playoffs –– one that has felt reminiscent of his historic struggles last October, and been further marred by a consequential ABS challenge he missed in Game 1.
While Roberts said he feels Pages has been “trying to do too much” –– downplaying any lingering effects from the fractured hand that sidelined the center fielder for most of September –– he also said he wanted to give the 25-year-old slugger more leash.
“I believe in him,” Roberts said. “And I feel that for us to win the World Series this year, we’re gonna need him to be an active part of our team.”
That was all part of the balance Roberts was trying to strike with his team’s season potentially hanging in the balance. It might still feel early for drastic changes. But one more loss, and the club’s three-peat bid will be on the brink.
“Our guys are our guys,” Roberts said. “Yeah, I can tweak a lineup. I can kind of insert, take out a player or two. But at the end of the day, we still have got to go out there and play and execute and take good at-bats.”

item.description: PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk. The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz. item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- The two-time defending World Series champions are in a rare funk.
The Los Angeles Dodgers lost their season-high seventh game in a row in a stunning collapse Friday night after the Arizona Diamondbacks rallied for a 4-3 win when rookie Ryan Waldschmidt hit a two-run, walk-off homer against closer Edwin Diaz.
"A loss is a loss, but to get walked off never feels good," Dodgers manager Dave Roberts said. "We didn't play a clean game, a great game, on either side of the baseball, but we did enough to put ourselves in position to win a game.
"Unfortunately, we couldn't finish it."
It was another rough outing for Diaz, who has an 11.00 ERA over 11 outings this season. The 32-year-old is a three-time All-Star, but he hasn't helped the Dodgers much after signing a three-year, $69 million deal during the offseason.
Waldschmidt connected on Diaz's hanging slider, hitting it into the left-center field seats for his second career homer and first big league walk-off.
"It's the slider," Diaz said. "The fastball was great today, but I missed the slider right in the middle. I think I was trying to be perfect with the pitch, and I'm missing right in the middle. I've got to be better. I'm a big league pitcher, so I've got to make pitches."
The Dodgers were swept by the Boston Red Sox and Chicago Cubs coming into Friday night's game. They still have a comfortable lead in the National League West -- 7 games in front of the Diamondbacks -- despite a 10-16 record since July 5.
Roberts acknowledged that Diaz has been struggling since his return from the injured list on July 29, but the manager wasn't necessarily ready to try a new closer. His reasoning was simple: There's no clear-cut alternative.
"Honestly, you've got to look at the options," Roberts said. "The way some of these guys are throwing, they're not throwing great either."
The Dodgers still look like a formidable team, particularly after adding ace left-hander Tarik Skubal in a trade-deadline deal with the Detroit Tigers last week. Two-time Cy Young Award winner Blake Snell is slated to return Tuesday after missing most of the season because of injuries.
And the lineup still has plenty of star power with Shohei Ohtani, Freddie Freeman, Mookie Betts and Kyle Tucker.
Roberts said before Friday's game that the remedy for the recent troubles was simple.
"We've just got to play better," Roberts said. "I don't think the standings -- I mean they're important, they matter -- but I just feel like with the talent we have, we've just got to play good baseball and it'll take care of itself. It always does."br/]

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Shohei Ohtani Could Move Further Down Lineup Amid Underperformance
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma

Ohtani is 2-for-8 this postseason, but that isn’t the worrying part. During the second game of the NLDS, Ohtani struggled to find the plate discipline he’s had throughout his career. item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers manager Dave Roberts revealed he’s willing to move Shohei Ohtani further down the lineup as his struggles in the box persist.
Ohtani is 2-for-8 this postseason, but that isn’t the worrying part. During the second game of the NLDS, Ohtani struggled to find the plate discipline he’s had throughout his career. He swung at 11 pitches while facing just 19, and chased on 53% of those swings.
He didn’t have the same struggles in Game 1, chasing at a rate of just 17%, but his performance in Game 2 was enough to prompt some questions regarding his fitness. The Dodgers have already moved Ohtani down in the order following his return from injury, running him out at the No. 2 spot several times since he came back, and Roberts revealed he’s open to dropping him further in the lineup.
“Going further than moving him from one to two, I’m open to it,” Roberts said. “If it’s something I do, I’d obviously have the conversation with Shohei to explain why. Every conversation I’ve had with him that’s whatever is best for the team, he’s all in on it.
Ohtani will remain in the lineup for the Dodgers’ Game 3 matchup against the Atlanta Braves regardless of his spot in the lineup, but faces a big challenge in the form of Chris Sale.
Is Chris Sale a Good Matchup for Shohei Ohtani?
The Dodgers are showing plenty of confidence in Ohtani by starting him on Tuesday, as Sale is a difficult matchup for the reigning MVP—especially given his recent struggles.
Sale ranked in the Top 5% of MLB With a 36.5% chase rate this season, strikes out batters at an extremely high clip and also throws from the left side, making at-bats for Ohtani inherently more difficult.
Ohtani will have to perform much better than he has since his return from injury in order to keep up with Sale, who performed incredibly against the Dodgers across two starts in the regular season, and the Dodgers need him to do so if they’re to avoid falling behind in the series.
The third game of the NLDS begins Tuesday at 3:00 p.m. PT.

item.title: [Dodgers Nation] Andy Pages' October Struggles Resurfacing at Worst Time
item.dc:creator: Aaron Coloma
item.description: Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages struggled in the 2025 postseason, making headlines for his poor performance, and his 2026 postseason so far hasn’t unfolded much differently. The outfielder is ordinarily a key producer for the Dodgers, and had a fantastic season in 2025 prior to his October breakdown. He hit 27 homers last year, good for second on the team behind Shohei Ohtani, and drove in 86 runs with a .774 OPS. Pages played in 16 games last postseason, stepping up to the plate 55 ti
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Dodgers outfielder Andy Pages struggled in the 2025 postseason, making headlines for his poor performance, and his 2026 postseason so far hasn’t unfolded much differently.
The outfielder is ordinarily a key producer for the Dodgers, and had a fantastic season in 2025 prior to his October breakdown. He hit 27 homers last year, good for second on the team behind Shohei Ohtani, and drove in 86 runs with a .774 OPS.
Pages played in 16 games last postseason, stepping up to the plate 55 times, and logged just four hits throughout the entirety of the postseason for a .078/.113/.098 slash line and a .211 OPS.
Now, through two games, his struggles are resurfacing.
What Has Andy Pages Done in the Playoffs This Year?
Through his two postseason games so far, Pages is hitless with one walk in eight plate appearances with four strikeouts. The strikeouts are the most worrying part of Pages’ performances so far this postseason, as he doesn’t ordinarily go down on strikes this often.
On the year, Pages’ strikeout rate sat at 19.7%, which is above league average and better than seasons past. Additionally, his whiff rate sits at 22.1%, also above league average. In his small sample size this postseason, though, both numbers are well above his yearly average with a 50% strikeout rate and a whiff rate of 36.4%.
Three of his four strikeouts came during the first game of the series, swinging and missing to record the last strike twice while watching strike three fly over the plate before wasting a challenge in the other. After Game 1, manager Dave Roberts revealed the Dodgers took away Pages’ green light to challenge.
“We talked a lot this year about Andy’s success rate or lack thereof, and I didn’t revisit it before Game 1, so that’s my fault,” Roberts said to the media, including Dodgers Nation, ahead of Game 2 on Sunday. “I did have a conversation today, so we’ve managed that one going forward.”
He also lined out in the first game of the series, hitting a ball 96.5 mph to center with a favorable launch angle—a promising sight given his struggles.
Pages yielded better results in the second game of the series, though not by much. He struck out for the fourth time this postseason in the second inning, but followed that up with a walk. In his final two at-bats of the game, he grounded out to either side of the middle infield.
The first-time All-Star ordinarily had solid quality of contact over the course of the season, and will hope to find his regular season form as the Dodgers make their three-peat push.
What Options Do the Dodgers Have to Replace Pages if His Struggles Continue?
The Dodgers aren’t likely to move away from Pages during this postseason, but if worst comes to worst, they have options to put in center over him. Tommy Edman is fully healthy and more than capable of manning the role, as is Hyeseong Kim.
Josue De Paula is also with the team at the moment, and could push a corner outfielder into center field if the Dodgers want to give him a game.
The Dodgers will hope they won’t have to do that, though, as Pages is a key player for them both on offense and defense. His next opportunity to break out of his small slump comes in Game 3 of the NLDS on Tuesday against Chris Sale.
